questions.topic: A conclusion about the future drawn from two facts about the present

options.text: The two facts may be unrelated, and without a link between them no forecast follows
The conclusion is fine, because a doubling population always ends in crowding
options.misconception: assumes that crowding is the only possible outcome of growth

options.text: The conclusion is wrong, because two degrees is a small rise in a tank
options.misconception: dismisses the facts as too small to matter rather than testing the link

options.text: The conclusion should be worded more carefully, but its direction is certain
options.misconception: treats a forecast as sound once the wording is tidied

questions.explanation: Two facts support a prediction only if something connects them. Temperature and population size may vary independently, so without a stated link the forecast is a guess with two facts attached.
questions.hint: Ask what connects the two facts.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A valid argument with a false conclusion
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an argument can be valid while its conclusion is false
questions.stem: A marine biologist argues: 'No filter can keep a marine tank under 8 mg per litre of ammonia; my filter keeps it at 9, so no filter can keep it under 9.' Explain why this argument is valid but its conclusion is false.

answer.exemplar: The form is sound: if no filter keeps ammonia below 8, and this filter leaves 9, then indeed no filter keeps it below 9, because 9 is above 8. But the conclusion is false, since a well-run tank with live rock and matured filter bacteria often holds ammonia near zero. The premises may also be false: plenty of filters do hold a tank under 8. Validity guarantees that true premises would give a true conclusion, not that the premises or the conclusion are true.

questions.explanation: Validity concerns the form of the inference, not the truth of its parts. The reasoning here is sound, so the false conclusion must come from a false premise or a false reading of a term.
questions.hint: Ask whether the premises are true.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A claim no result could count against
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a claim with no fixed measure cannot be tested
questions.stem: A marine biologist's tank note states: 'This strain of copepod is the most heat-tolerant strain available to hobbyists.' Explain why no experimental result could count against this claim.

answer.exemplar: The claim contains no measure that a result could come out against. 'Most heat-tolerant' is not defined by a temperature, a survival rate or a duration, so any experiment can be described as consistent with it by adjusting the criterion afterwards. It also compares against 'available to hobbyists', a stock that changes as strains are bred and sold. A claim that no result could count against is not so much false as unable to be tested, and it should be re-expressed with a specified measure before it can be checked.

questions.explanation: A claim that no result could count against has no fixed measure and no fixed comparison set, so any outcome can be absorbed into it. Such a claim is untestable rather than merely untrue.
questions.hint: Ask what a result would have to show to fail.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A claim no result could count against
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a claim with no specified intervention cannot be tested
questions.stem: A tank note claims: 'Stress in marine fish is best managed by improving water quality.' Explain why no experimental result could count against this claim.

answer.exemplar: The claim has no specified measure, no specified intervention and no specified outcome, so every experiment can be described without contradicting it. A trial showing that adding a vitamin improved survival fits, and a trial showing that changing water quality made no difference also fits, because the terms 'improving', 'quality' and 'managed' can be set after the fact. The claim functions as an expectation rather than a proposition. To become checkable it must name an intervention, an outcome and a comparison.

questions.explanation: A claim that no result could count against has no fixed intervention, measure or comparison, so any outcome can be fitted to it afterwards. Such a claim is an expectation rather than a testable proposition.
questions.hint: Ask what a result would have to look like to fail it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A valid argument with true premises
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an argument with checked premises and a sound form is reliable
questions.stem: A marine biologist writes: 'Every water sample in this survey was filtered through 0.45 micron filters, so the reported bacterial counts are comparable across sites.' Explain why this argument is valid and its premises true.

answer.exemplar: The argument is valid because the conclusion follows directly from the stated condition: counts obtained by the same method can be compared, and counts obtained by different methods cannot. The premise is true because the sampling log records that every site was sampled with the same filter type on every visit, with the filter changed between samples as the protocol requires. questions.explanation: The inference is sound because the conclusion follows from the single stated condition, and the sampling log confirms that the condition held on every visit. Both parts can be checked by a reader.
questions.hint: Ask what the condition alone licenses.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A valid argument with true premises
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sampling rule makes a set of records usable
questions.stem: A marine biologist writes: 'Every colony photographed for the survey was located by the same systematic transect rule, so no colony in the survey area was missed on grounds of visibility or choice.' Explain why this argument is valid and its premises true.

answer.exemplar: The argument is valid because the conclusion is licensed by the premise alone: a systematic rule applied to every colony leaves the location of colonies to the rule rather than to the observer, and so removes both visibility bias and the observer's choice. The premise is true because the field log records the transect positions, the order of visits and the photography at each position. A reader can therefore check that the rule was followed and rely on the conclusion that the survey missed nothing.

questions.explanation: The inference is sound because the conclusion follows from the single stated condition, and the field log confirms that the rule was applied at every position. Both parts are open to checking by a reader.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule alone guarantees.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A summary that leaves out the detail qualifying it
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a summary of a conditional finding misleads
questions.stem: A tank report summarises an experiment as: 'Added iron reduced the growth of the algae.' The underlying data note that the reduction occurred only where the water was already above 20 mg per litre of nitrate. Explain the effect of the summary on a reader.

answer.exemplar: The summary converts a conditional finding into an unconditional one. In the data, the effect of added iron was conditional on the nitrate level already being high, so iron and nitrate together produced the reduction. A reader working from the summary will predict that adding iron will reduce growth in any tank, and will be surprised in a low-nitrate tank where nothing happens. The summary has also implied that iron was the operative factor, where the data suggest a combination.

questions.explanation: The summary states an effect without the condition under which it held, and implies iron acted alone where the data point to a combination. The reader is left with a rule that will fail in most tanks.
questions.hint: Ask what had to be true for the effect.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A citation that supports a weaker claim than the one made
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a citation establishes for a claim about causes
questions.stem: A marine biologist writes: 'Rising sea temperatures are the cause of coral bleaching across the region, as the single-lagoon study shows.' Explain what this citation establishes.

answer.exemplar: The study establishes that a heat spike bleached colonies at one lagoon in one summer, and that nearby colonies at the same mean temperature did not bleach. It does not establish a regional cause, because it covered one site, one season and one event, and the draft says nothing about the controls that would be needed to attribute the region's bleaching to temperature rather than to local conditions. The citation therefore supports a narrower claim about a mechanism than the sentence asserts.

questions.explanation: The citation carries the authority of a study onto a claim the study never tested. A single lagoon in a single summer can show that heat spikes bleach corals, but not that temperature causes bleaching across a region.
questions.hint: Ask what the study measured and where.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A citation that supports a weaker claim than the one made
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a citation establishes for a predictive threshold claim
questions.stem: A tank essay states: 'Nitrate above 40 mg per litre will trigger disease in any reef aquarium.' It cites a paper reporting disease in one system whose nitrate exceeded 40. Explain what the citation establishes.

answer.exemplar: The paper establishes that disease appeared in one system whose nitrate was above 40, and it may establish an association there. It does not establish that nitrate above 40 will trigger disease in any reef aquarium, because a single system cannot supply the universal reach the sentence claims, and the paper may not have controlled for temperature, stocking or husbandry. As a result the citation lends the authority of a study to a general claim the study never tested, which is what makes the sentence overstated.

questions.explanation: The citation supports an association in one system, while the sentence asserts a universal trigger. The source is on the right subject but reaches nowhere near as far as the claim attached to it.
questions.hint: Ask how many systems the source examined.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A passage that persuades without arguing
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a passage appeals to what a readership already accepts
questions.stem: A tank newsletter writes: 'Ask anyone who keeps marine tanks and they will tell you the skimmer is essential.' Explain how this passage persuades and why it does not argue.

answer.exemplar: The passage appeals to the agreement of other keepers and treats that agreement as sufficient to move the reader. It offers no premise about how skimmers work, no evidence about ammonia or organics, and nothing against which a reader could check the claim. The reference to other keepers also shifts attention away from the merits of the advice and towards the company the reader keeps. Because nothing is put forward to assess, the passage persuades without arguing, however true the advice may be.

questions.explanation: The passage invites the reader to rely on other keepers' agreement and gives no premise to assess. That is persuasion by consensus, and it is not an argument however sound the advice might be.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is asked to take on trust.

answer.exemplar: The post works by two appeals at once. The phrase 'everyone in this forum knows it' invites the reader to treat agreement as proof, and 'honestly' presents the speaker as candid rather than commercial. Neither appeal offers anything the reader could evaluate: no mechanism, no measurement, no comparison of skimmered and unskimmered tanks. The post therefore moves the reader by shared belief and by tone. Its advice may well be right, but a reader has been persuaded rather than given a reason to accept it.

questions.explanation: The post appeals to agreement in the forum and to the speaker's candour, and it offers no premise to assess. That is persuasion, and it leaves the reader no way to test the advice.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is asked to take on trust.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A counterexample that does not refute
questions.learningObjective: Assess a proposed counterexample against the claim's own terms

stimulus.body: Comment on my essay: 'Every marine aquarium needs a protein skimmer.' A reader replies: I keep a fish-only tank with no rock, no sand and no skimmer, and the fish have lived three years. My definition of a marine aquarium requires live rock, so the reader's tank is not one.

questions.stem: What is the best assessment of the reader's reply?

options.text: It is a refutation, because three years is long enough to show skimmers are unneeded
options.misconception: treats a short period as decisive for a claim about practice

options.text: It is not a refutation, because the tank falls outside the class the claim is about
It is a refutation, because the tank survived without a skimmer
options.misconception: ignores whether the case is an instance of the claim

options.text: It is not a refutation, because the claim concerns skimmers rather than tank types
options.misconception: misidentifies what the claim is about

questions.explanation: The claim is about marine aquariums, and the essay defines those as tanks with live rock. The reader's tank is outside that class, so the case provides no evidence about skimmers in the tanks the claim is about.
questions.hint: Ask what the claim's own definition covers.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A claim no result could count against
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a claim about fault cannot be settled by evidence
questions.stem: A tank note claims: 'Most problems in marine aquaria are the keeper's fault.' Which assessment of this claim is right?

options.text: It is testable, because keeper error can be established by checking the log
options.misconception: supposes one record can settle a general attribution

options.text: It is testable, because comparing faultful and careful keepers would settle it
options.misconception: supplies a test the claim's wording would not survive

options.text: It is not testable, because it names no measure of fault and no defined class of problems
It is not testable, because it is a personal view rather than a factual claim
options.misconception: grounds untestability in the personal voice rather than in vagueness

questions.explanation: The claim names neither a measure of fault nor a defined class of problems, so any failure can be assigned to the keeper after the fact. Vagueness, not the personal voice, is what makes the claim immune to evidence.
questions.hint: Ask how 'most' and 'fault' would be measured.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A summary that leaves out the detail qualifying it
questions.learningObjective: Judge a summary that drops both a condition and a second difference
questions.stem: A quarterly summary states: 'Enriching the water with iron improved coral growth.' The detailed entry records that growth improved only where nitrate was already high, and that the enriched tanks also received additional light. Which judgement is right?

options.text: The summary is fair, because it reports the direction of the result accurately
options.misconception: ignores the conditions that bound the result

options.text: The summary is fair, because it names iron, the variable that was manipulated
options.misconception: treats naming the manipulated variable as sufficient for fairness

options.text: The summary is unfair, because it should give the percentage change in growth
options.misconception: demands a figure the record never provides

options.text: The summary is unfair, because it drops the nitrate condition and the added light

questions.explanation: A summary that omits both the condition under which the effect appeared and a second difference between the tanks lets the reader infer a simple causal story that the detail does not support.
questions.hint: List what the summary dropped.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A citation that supports a weaker claim than the one made
questions.learningObjective: Describe the effect of citing a source that establishes less than the claim
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a citation that supports a weaker claim than the one made?

options.text: The source is irrelevant, so the citation should simply be deleted from the essay
options.misconception: overstates the mismatch as total irrelevance

options.text: The source is wrong, so the citation refutes the claim it is attached to
options.misconception: confuses a weaker source with a contradictory one

options.text: The claim is right and the source is old, so the citation should be updated
options.misconception: treats recency as the only problem a citation can have

options.text: The source establishes less than the claim, so the citation lends support the claim has not earned

questions.explanation: A citation transfers credibility from the source to the claim. When the source established less than the claim, that transfer makes the argument look supported where it is not, which is the sense in which it is overstated.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader will think has been shown.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A conclusion about the future drawn from two facts about the present
questions.learningObjective: Identify the weakness in a forecast that fixes a timetable it cannot support

stimulus.body: Logged this morning: the corals look pale compared with last month, and the water temperature is 27 degrees, two above my usual setting. My prediction is that they will bleach within a week.

questions.stem: What is the main weakness in this log entry's prediction?

options.text: The forecast attaches a specific timetable to facts that establish no mechanism at all
The forecast is too strong, because a two-degree rise can never harm coral
options.misconception: asserts a guarantee that contradicts the logged concern

options.text: The forecast is fine, since the coral's paleness confirms the temperature as the cause
options.misconception: treats an accompanying sign as proof of a mechanism

options.text: The forecast should use the word 'might' rather than 'will' to be accurate
options.misconception: suggests a wording fix where the reasoning is at fault

questions.explanation: Two present observations do not by themselves supply a mechanism, and nothing in the log fixes how soon a bleaching event would follow. The prediction therefore claims both a cause and a deadline that the record has not earned.
questions.hint: Ask what the log actually establishes about timing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A valid argument with a false conclusion
questions.learningObjective: Select an argument that reaches a false conclusion by valid reasoning
questions.stem: Which of these arguments reaches a false conclusion by valid reasoning?

options.text: My tank has corals and no heater, so aquariums do not need heaters
options.misconception: infers a universal from a single case that may not be one

options.text: No aquarium can hold corals without a heater; my tank has corals and no heater; so it cannot hold corals
Corals in heated tanks are healthy, so tanks without heat cannot be kept
options.misconception: reaches a true general claim by invalid reasoning

options.text: No aquarium can hold corals without heat, so coral keeping is impossible
options.misconception: overstates the conclusion in a way the premises do not license

questions.explanation: The second argument is valid: if no aquarium can hold corals without a heater and this one has neither corals nor a heater, then it cannot hold corals. The premise is false, since aquariums do exist without heaters, and that makes the conclusion false too.
questions.hint: Ask whether the form works and the premises hold.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A valid argument with true premises
questions.learningObjective: Assess an argument whose shared method licenses its comparison
questions.stem: A marine biologist reasons: 'Every tank in the trial was filtered the same way, so the nitrate readings are comparable.' Which assessment of this argument is right?

options.text: The reasoning is valid, but its premises turn out to be false in the record
options.misconception: asserts falsity without pointing to any evidence

options.text: The reasoning is invalid, because comparability is not the same as identity
options.misconception: attacks a sound form by conflating two different ideas

options.text: The reasoning is invalid, because a shared method cannot make readings comparable
options.misconception: denies what a shared method plainly does license

options.text: The reasoning is valid and its premises are true, so the conclusion is sound

questions.explanation: The inference draws only what the stated condition warrants, and the trial record confirms that the filtration was identical in every tank. Both the reasoning and the facts hold, so the comparison can be relied on.
questions.hint: Ask what the shared method licenses.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A passage that persuades without arguing
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a persuasive passage from an argumentative one
questions.stem: What distinguishes a persuasive passage from an argumentative one in a marine tank article?

options.text: An argumentative passage is always longer than a persuasive one
options.misconception: confuses length with the presence of reasons

options.text: A persuasive passage is always written in the first person
options.misconception: attaches a stylistic feature to a logical distinction

options.text: An argumentative passage always recommends a specific course of action
options.misconception: confuses a practical recommendation with the presence of reasoning

options.text: An argumentative passage puts premises on the table that a reader can assess

questions.explanation: An argument can be assessed because it lays out premises that can be checked and a conclusion that follows or does not. Persuasion works through other routes, so the reader is moved without anything to evaluate.
questions.hint: Ask whether premises are on the table.
